text: Persons experiencing homelessness (PEH) are at higher risk for SARS-CoV-2 infection and severe illness due to COVID-19 because of a limited ability to physically distance and a higher burden of underlying health conditions.
label: BACKGROUND

text: To describe and assess a hotel-based protective housing intervention to reduce incidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection among PEH in Chicago, Illinois, with increased risk of severe illness due to COVID-19.
label: CLAIM

text: This retrospective cohort study analyzed PEH who were provided protective housing in individual hotel rooms in downtown Chicago during the COVID-19 pandemic from April 2 through September 3, 2020.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Participants were PEH at increased risk for severe COVID-19, defined as (1) aged at least 60 years regardless of health conditions, (2) aged at least 55 years with any underlying health condition posing increased risk, or (3) aged less than 55 years with any underlying health condition posing substantially increased risk (eg, HIV/AIDS).
label: BACKGROUND

text: Participants were housed in individual hotel rooms to reduce the risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection; on-site health care workers provided daily symptom monitoring, regular SARS-CoV-2 testing, and care for chronic health conditions.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Additional on-site services included treatment of mental health and substance use disorders and social services.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The main outcome measured was SARS-CoV-2 incidence, with SARS-Cov2 infection defined as a positive upper respiratory specimen using any polymerase chain reaction diagnostic assay authorized for emergency use by the Food and Drug Administration.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Secondary outcomes were blood pressure control, glycemic control as measured by hemoglobin A1c, and housing placements at departure.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Of 259 participants from 16 homeless shelters in Chicago, 104 (40.2%) were aged at least 65 years, 190 (73.4%) were male, 185 (71.4%) were non-Hispanic Black, and 49 (18.9%) were non-Hispanic White.
label: BACKGROUND

text: There was an observed reduction in SARS-CoV-2 incidence during the study period among the protective housing cohort (54.7 per 1000 people [95% CI, 22.4-87.1 per 1000 people]) compared with citywide rates for PEH residing in shelters (137.1 per 1000 people [95% CI, 125.1-149.1 per 1000 people]; P = .001).
label: CLAIM

text: There was also an adjusted change in systolic blood pressure at a rate of −5.7 mm Hg (95% CI, −9.3 to −2.1 mm Hg) and hemoglobin A1c at a rate of −1.4% (95% CI, −2.4% to −0.4%) compared with baseline.
label: CLAIM

text: More than half of participants (51% [n = 132]) departed from the intervention to housing of some kind (eg, supportive housing).
label: CLAIM

text: This cohort study found that protective housing was associated with a reduction in SARS-CoV-2 infection among high-risk PEH during the first wave of the COVID-19 pandemic in Chicago.
label: CLAIM

text: These findings suggest that with appropriate wraparound supports (ie, multisector services to address complex needs), such housing interventions may reduce the risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection, improve noncommunicable disease control, and provide a pathway to permanent housing.
label: CLAIM

text: Persons experiencing homelessness (PEH) are at increased risk of becoming infected with SARS-CoV-2 and developing COVID-19.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Studies across the US and Europe have identified a high incidence of SARS-CoV-2 in PEH, particularly among those in congregate settings.[1],[2],[3],[4]
label: BACKGROUND

text: In one early study conducted at a large homeless shelter in Boston,[1] more than one-third of residents (36%) tested positive for SARS-CoV-2, the majority (88%) of whom were asymptomatic at the time of testing.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Difficulty maintaining physical distance, as well as challenges in obtaining personal protective equipment, can make SARS-CoV-2 transmission more likely among PEH.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Importantly, PEH also have a higher prevalence of underlying health conditions that place them at higher risk for severe illness or death from COVID-19.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The prevalence of hypertension is estimated to be 50% among PEH in the US,[5] with multiple studies documenting poor rates of blood pressure control.[6],[7],[8]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Although prevalence of diabetes in PEH may be comparable with other low-income populations,[5] the likelihood of adequate glucose control is substantially lower[9] resulting in higher complication rates.[10]
label: BACKGROUND

text: In April 2020, a hotel-based protective housing intervention was implemented in Chicago, Illinois, through a joint effort by the Chicago Departments of Public Health (CDPH), Family and Support Services (DFSS), and Housing (DOH), in conjunction with Lawndale Christian Health Center (LCHC), a federally qualified health center with longstanding experience in providing health care to PEH.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Published assessments of interventions elsewhere have focused on widespread testing to interrupt transmission of COVID-19 in congregate settings,[4],[11] or isolation and quarantine measures for PEH who tested positive.[12]
label: BACKGROUND

text: This Chicago model, in contrast, provided protective housing for PEH who were at risk for severe illness and death from COVID-19 owing to older age or underlying health conditions.
label: BACKGROUND

text: We are not aware of any published assessments of similar protective housing efforts.
label: BACKGROUND

text: In addition to individualized hotel rooms, on-site health care workers provided symptom monitoring, regular SARS-CoV-2 testing, and medical care for chronic health conditions.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Other key services included meal delivery, treatment of mental health and substance use disorders (SUDs), as well as social services.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Although hotel conversions to expand supportive housing existed before the pandemic, the COVID-19 pandemic provided an accelerated opportunity to pilot a model targeted to PEH with high-risk health conditions.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The primary aim of this study was to describe Chicago’s hotel-based protective housing intervention and assess whether the intervention was associated with any differences in the incidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection among those participating in the intervention relative to the citywide population of sheltered PEH.
label: CLAIM

text: Secondary aims were to assess change in high-risk health conditions during the study period, including hypertension and diabetes; describe treatment for mental health conditions and SUDs; and describe housing outcomes on departure from the intervention.
label: CLAIM

text: The prevalence of mental illness is high among homeless populations, yet traditional clinic-based care is often inaccessible.
label: BACKGROUND

text: For urban areas where housing-first models are difficult to implement because of high costs, integrated on-site psychiatric services in shelters may offer a feasible alternative.
label: BACKGROUND

text: To examine clinical and demographic factors associated with housing attainment among individuals experiencing homelessness with mental illness participating in an on-site psychiatric service program.
label: BACKGROUND

text: This 5-year retrospective cohort study analyzed data collected from October 2019 to October 2024.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The study was conducted at the only public temporary shelter in Taipei, Taiwan.
label: BACKGROUND

text: A sample of individuals with mental illness who voluntarily joined the program was identified.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Participants received integrated on-site psychiatric care through the Psychiatric Assistance for Transitional Homelessness in Shelters (PATHS) program, which included psychiatric assessment, pharmacological treatment, access to social welfare, and referrals for psychiatric hospitalization, all delivered within the shelter setting.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The primary outcome was housing attainment, defined a priori as relocation to residential psychiatric rehabilitation facilities, original family, or rental house upon shelter exit.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Categorical variables were compared using χ^2 and Fisher exact tests.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Of 231 individuals initially identified, 3 individuals who died and 20 who remained in the shelter at the end of the study were excluded.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Among the 208 included participants (90.0% of the initial sample; median [IQR] age, 54.0 [44.3-62.0] years; 154 male [74.0%]), alcohol use disorder predominated among men, whereas women had a higher prevalence of schizophrenia.
label: CLAIM

text: Overall, 97 participants (46.6%) attained housing.
label: CLAIM

text: Older age was significantly associated with housing attainment (odds ratio [OR], 1.03; 95% CI, 1.01-1.05; P = .04).
label: CLAIM

text: In contrast, alcohol use disorder (OR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.29-0.99; P = .045) and opioid or methamphetamine use disorders (OR, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.14-0.62; P = .001) were associated with lower likelihood of housing attainment.
label: CLAIM

text: In this retrospective cohort study of 208 homeless individuals with mental illness, on-site psychiatric services provided a framework for bridging the gap between transitional shelters and housing attainment.
label: CLAIM

text: These findings suggest that transitioning from universal models toward individualized interventions is essential to address the diverse needs of this population and improve housing success.
label: CLAIM

text: Homelessness remains a pressing social issue worldwide, prompting both governmental and nongovernmental organizations to develop intervention strategies.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The multifaceted nature of homelessness is closely linked to economic challenges, inadequate social support systems, and public health concerns, particularly regarding the high burden of mental illness.[1],[2]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Mental illness is significantly more prevalent among individuals experiencing homelessness than in the general population,[3],[4],[5],[6] with prevalence estimated to be as high as 67% to 76%.[7],[8]
label: BACKGROUND

text: The presence of comorbid mental disorders has been associated with worse outcomes, including a 70% increase in mortality risk,[9] higher rates of criminal behavior and victimization,[10],[11] and longer durations of homelessness.[12]
label: BACKGROUND

text: However, since most mental disorders are treatable, they present a valuable opportunity to reduce health disparities through targeted interventions.[13],[14]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Evidence suggests conventional clinic-based models of care that require unhoused patients to attend mental health appointments regularly and on time are not ideal.[6],[15]
label: BACKGROUND

text: As a result, the current approach for intervention programs in individuals experiencing homelessness with mental disorders has been shifted from the traditional treatment-first model, which required treatment before housing, to the housing-first (HF) model.
label: BACKGROUND

text: This newer approach first provides stable housing and then offers recovery-oriented support through assertive community treatment teams, a method that has been shown to more reliably secure long-term housing.[16],[17],[18],[19],[20]
label: BACKGROUND

text: However, studies have shown that no significant differences were observed for psychiatric symptoms severity between HF group and treatment-as-usual group (ie, only receiving existing support and social services).[17],[21],[22]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Therefore, the HF model alone may be insufficient, and its success hinges on implementation, specifically the tailored type, and high quality and sufficient intensity of support services, to ensure long-term housing stability.[20],[22],[23],[24],[25]
label: CLAIM

text: Implementing the HF model in Taipei City, located in a metropolitan area in Taiwan, faces economic difficulties.
label: BACKGROUND

text: In 2024, Taipei ranked 17th globally for housing unaffordability among cities, with a price-to-income ratio of 28.8.[26]
label: BACKGROUND

text: In this context, the city faces substantial challenges in supporting its estimated 700 to 800 individuals experiencing homelessness.
label: BACKGROUND

text: These challenges include a lack of public housing to implement an HF model, limited rental subsidies, and low public support for prioritizing this population over other vulnerable groups.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Yuang-Tong House, the only public temporary homeless shelter operated by the Taipei City Department of Social Welfare, is one of the few social housing facilities available for individuals experiencing homelessness, but it previously did not provide psychiatric services.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Unpublished internal data from Yuang-Tong House (provided by coauthor Y.C.P., who is the director of Yuang-Tong House) indicate that fewer than one-quarter of its residents were able to achieve housing attainment through the support of social workers alone.
label: BACKGROUND

text: This rate is even lower among those with co-occurring mental illness.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Research shows that integrating psychiatric services with housing support substantially improves engagement in care for this population.[27]
label: BACKGROUND

text: To address this unmet need, the Psychiatric Assistance for Transitional Homelessness in Shelters (PATHS) program was established in 2019.
label: BACKGROUND

text: The PATHS program delivers on-site psychiatric services at Yuang-Tong House, aiming to directly address residents’ mental health needs, enhance their access to care, and ensure that their homeless status does not impede treatment delivery.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Although factors such as case management assistance and younger age often facilitate shelter exit, others, including chronic homelessness and criminal records, frequently emerge as substantial barriers in international studies.[12],[28]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Against this backdrop, the PATHS program recognizes the bidirectional nature of mental health and housing instability, in alignment with established evidence.[29],[30],[31]
label: BACKGROUND

text: However, most existing literature focuses on the general severity of psychological symptoms rather than structured psychiatric diagnostic interviews,[32],[33],[34] leaving the relationship between specific psychiatric diagnoses and housing outcomes largely unexplored.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Although determining whether mental illness was the primary driver of the initial onset of homelessness remains challenging, the PATHS program’s longitudinal framework allows for the systematic tracking of participants’ status.
label: BACKGROUND

text: In this 5-year observational cohort study, we followed individuals experiencing homelessness at the shelter to characterize their trajectories and to identify factors associated with shelter exit outcomes.
label: BACKGROUND

text: We also examined the forms of housing attainment and identified the variables explaining each outcome.
label: BACKGROUND

text: In particular, we assessed each participant’s psychiatric diagnoses, as defined by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (Fifth Edition), to evaluate the impact of comorbid mental health conditions on shelter exit outcomes.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Accordingly, this study aimed to determine the housing attainment rate for individuals experiencing homelessness with mental illness under the PATHS program and to identify the clinical and demographic factors associated with successful housing attainment.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Managed alcohol programs (MAPs) are harm reduction services that provide regular, measured doses of beverage-grade alcohol alongside social and health services, aiming to reduce nonbeverage alcohol consumption and harms associated with excessive intoxication and withdrawal.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Most MAPs are paired with supportive housing, which can be at a single building (“single-site”) or more uncommonly across multiple apartments (“scattered-site”).
label: BACKGROUND

text: The North End Community Health Centre – Mobile Outreach Street Health (MOSH) in Halifax, Nova Scotia, established Atlantic Canada’s first MAP, using a scattered-site model, in April 2020 – during the COVID-19 pandemic.
label: BACKGROUND

text: We aimed to describe program participants, summarize outcomes, and understand stakeholder perceptions of program successes and challenges.
label: CLAIM

text: Parallel, mixed methods program evaluation.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Quantitative arm involved retrospective review of weekly program assessments documenting presence or absence of outcomes (April 2020-December 2022).
label: BACKGROUND

text: Qualitative arm included 4 focus groups with key stakeholders (May-June 2021).
label: BACKGROUND

text: Over the first 33 months, 38 people enrolled in MAP.
label: CLAIM

text: At the time of our study, 9 had died and 9 left the program.
label: CLAIM

text: Of the 20 remaining participants, 13 consented to chart review (92% male; age mean 46, SD 11 years) and 9 had weekly outcome data available.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Comparing year 1 to year 2, participants had mean person-week prevalence of any nonbeverage alcohol consumption (eg, hand sanitizer): 9% and 3%; acute alcohol-related harms: 25% and 9%; and seizures: 4% and 1%.
label: CLAIM

text: Mean person-week prevalence of out-of-program drinking was 34% in year 1 and 33% in year 2.
label: CLAIM

text: Focus groups highlighted MAP improved participants’ health and decreased frequency of nonbeverage alcohol consumption, survival behaviors, and violence.
label: CLAIM

text: Challenges included out-of-program drinking and lack of social programming.
label: CLAIM

text: This scattered-site MAP may support positive health and social outcomes for people with severe alcohol use disorder.
label: CLAIM

text: Identified program gaps can be explored to better meet participant needs and reduce out-of-program drinking.
label: CLAIM

text: Adults experiencing homelessness face disproportionate rates of chronic illness, trauma, mental illness, violence, and have higher rates of substance and alcohol use compared to the general population.[1]-[4]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Within Canada, between 37% to 73% of adults experiencing homelessness engage in heavy episodic or daily drinking (more than 20 standard drinks per day), interfering with their ability to access and maintain housing.[1]-[5]
label: BACKGROUND

text: People experiencing homelessness and alcohol use disorder face risks of alcohol-related injuries, exposure to extreme environmental elements, theft, or exploitation;[2],[4],[5] people with limited income may need to consume low-cost nonbeverage alcohol (NBA; eg, mouthwash; hand sanitizer) or to engage in theft to obtain alcohol.[4],[6],[7]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Beyond individual harms, this results in substantial health and social costs, ambulance and emergency department utilization, hospitalizations, and frequent police encounters.[1],[3],[5],[7],[8]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Heavy alcohol consumption is also associated with increased rates of mental illness, poor physical health, and chronic diseases,[1],[4]-[6] as well as alcohol-related harms including withdrawal, seizures, alcohol-related injuries, and alcohol-related mortality.[3]-[5],[7]
label: BACKGROUND

text: As a result, people experiencing homelessness and alcohol use disorders are a priority population for equity-seeking health initiatives.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Managed alcohol programs (MAPs) are harm reduction services for individuals with severe alcohol use disorder, particularly those experiencing homelessness.[2],[5],[9]-[13]
label: BACKGROUND

text: MAPs provide participants with regular, measured doses of beverage-grade alcohol at scheduled dispensing intervals to prevent withdrawal, reduce binge drinking episodes and public intoxication, and decrease NBA consumption and alcohol-related harms.[1]-[3],[6],[8],[10],[14]
label: BACKGROUND

text: They often provide housing and primary healthcare services, financial support, cultural programming, social services, and other programming.[2],[8]
label: BACKGROUND

text: These programs operate using various models including at residential single-sites, day programs, hospital-based, shelter-based, scattered-site (eg, across multiple housing units), or a mix of multiple settings.
label: BACKGROUND

text: MAP operational guidance documents were published for the province of British Columbia in 2020 [15] and nationally in Canada in 2023. [16]
label: BACKGROUND

text: In recent years, there has been a rapid increase in the number of MAPs operating in Canada – many catalyzed by the COVID-19 pandemic.
label: BACKGROUND

text: As of 2024, there were 44 MAPs in Canada operating within 8 provinces and 1 territory. [17]
label: BACKGROUND

text: MAPs have expanded across Canada more quickly than other jurisdictions; we are aware of few MAPs in international locations, including 2 in USA; 3 in Australia; and 1 in Spain.[18]-[20]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Limited uptake internationally may be due to several factors, including the need for further evidence evaluating different MAP models in different settings.
label: BACKGROUND

text: Evidence from a variety of Canadian models suggests MAPs may reduce frequency of binge drinking and NBA consumption, frequency and severity of withdrawal symptoms, and incidence of alcohol-related harms.[5],[7],[8],[10],[17],[21]
label: BACKGROUND

text: MAP participation is also associated with reduced police encounters.[3],[5],[7],[17],[18],[21]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Long-term MAP participation (defined by one study as enrollment for more than 2 months), was associated with increased engagement in primary healthcare services. [10]
label: BACKGROUND

text: MAPs are acceptable to participants, with residential-based models being viewed as dignified services that provide safety, increase perceived self-worth, and sense of control.[3],[4],[9],[12],[22]
label: BACKGROUND

text: These programs also facilitate opportunities for participants to positively engage with their community, develop therapeutic relationships with healthcare professionals and staff, and build, maintain, and repair family and social relationships.[3],[4],[7],[9],[17],[21]
label: BACKGROUND

text: Although an emerging evidence-base suggests MAPs are successful in supporting individuals with alcohol use disorder, there is especially limited evidence regarding “scattered-site” models of MAP, with outreach delivery of beverage-grade alcohol to multiple apartment or housing units (often with only 1-2 deliveries per day).
label: BACKGROUND

text: We are aware of only 4 other MAPs (located within British Columbia and Saskatchewan, Canada) that included scattered-site deliveries, but no published evaluations of scattered-site models.[11],[13],[17]
label: BACKGROUND

text: A recent scoping review specifically highlighted the need for more research on scattered-site MAP models. [11]
label: BACKGROUND

text: In April 2020, the Mobile Outreach Street Health (MOSH) program in Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada established a mixed model (scattered- and single-site) MAP on an emergency basis to support people with severe alcohol use disorder experiencing homelessness.
label: BACKGROUND

text: This included providing MAP at both a supportive housing residential site and a scattered-site model delivering alcohol to participants’ independent residences and COVID isolation shelters in the community.
label: BACKGROUND

text: This was established urgently during the first wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, in order to facilitate self-isolation and/or quarantine.[18],[22]
label: BACKGROUND

text: It is among Canada’s first mixed-scattered site MAP models, and, at the time, there was no national guidance for scattered-site programs.
label: BACKGROUND

text: It has since expanded beyond its initial scope to continue to be able to support people experiencing homelessness and severe alcohol use disorder in Halifax.
label: BACKGROUND

text: This evaluation serves to contribute to the emerging evidence-base regarding MAPs, address knowledge gaps surrounding scattered-site MAP delivery, and help inform future implementation of MAP models in other jurisdictions.
label: CLAIM

text: In this study, we aimed to describe MAP participants; summarize program outcomes (ie, out-of-program drinking, NBA consumption, and acute-alcohol related harms including blackouts, falls, physical altercations, seizures, and withdrawal symptoms); and understand stakeholder perceptions of the MAP’s successes and challenges.
label: CLAIM
